hook: The Spartan king who held the pass at Thermopylae with 300 men.

pages.x: As a younger son, Leonidas was never meant to be king, so he went through the agoge, the brutal training of Spartan boys. Taken from home at seven, they got one cloak a year, slept on reeds and were told to steal their food; they were punished only for getting caught. Leonidas became king around 490 BC after his half-brothers died.

In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with a huge army. Leonidas led about 7,000 Greeks, among them 300 Spartans, to Thermopylae, a narrow pass between the mountains and the sea. For two days they threw back wave after wave of Persians, even the king's elite Immortals.

Herodotus says a local man warned that the Persian archers were so many their arrows would hide the sun. "Good," replied a Spartan named Dienekes, "then we shall fight in the shade." Told to hand over their weapons, Leonidas is said to have answered "Molon labe": "Come and take them."

A Greek named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass. Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with his 300, with 700 men from Thespiae and some others. They fought to the last; when their spears broke they fought with swords, then with their hands. Xerxes had the dead king beheaded.
pages.cap: Leonidas at Thermopylae, by Jacques-Louis David

pages.x: The Greeks later put up a stone at the pass, with lines by the poet Simonides: "Go tell the Spartans, stranger passing by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie." Within a year, Greek victories at Salamis and Plataea drove the Persians out of Greece for good.

Leonidas lost his battle, but his stand bought time for the Greeks and became the most famous example of courage against overwhelming odds. For 2,500 years "the 300" have inspired soldiers, poets and filmmakers.
pts: Held the pass at Thermopylae against a vast Persian army
Died with his 300 Spartans rather than retreat
A symbol of courage against the odds
